clue.text: Such creatures stop short, one spot.

definitions.text: Such creatures stop short, one spot

parts.words: Such creatures stop short, one spot
parts.note: creatures whose tails stop short, all hailing from one spot, an island in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A naturalist notes some animals halting abruptly in one place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop short' sounds like halting, but it describes tails that are mere stumps; the 'one spot' is the Isle of Man, home of the breed.
explanation.definitionFit: The breed from the Isle of Man is famous for being tailless, its rear stopping in a stump.

clue.text: This weed is guaranteed to annoy.

definitions.meaning: a stinging plant of hedgerows and waste ground
to irritate or provoke someone, as if stung

explanation.surface: A gardener grumbles that a particular weed is certain to irritate.
explanation.definitionFit: The stinging plant gives its name to the verb meaning to irk or rile someone.

clue.text: Phase reformed by copper formed.

indicators.note: something reformed is made over in a new shape, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

parts.note: a copper coin was a penny, abbreviated d in old British money

explanation.surface: A stage of a process is reworked with copper to make something moulded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed' rearranges PHASE into SHAPE; the old British penny, a copper coin, was written d (from Latin denarius).
explanation.definitionFit: Something shaped has been given a form, so the two past participles are synonyms.

clue.text: Man with skill takes some beating!

parts.note: a man is referred to as he
art is skill, as in the art of conversation

explanation.surface: A skilful fellow is hard to beat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes some beating' usually means is hard to better; here it is literal, describing the organ that beats all day.
explanation.definitionFit: The organ pumping blood beats constantly, so it literally receives a great deal of beating.

clue.text: A—bank swelled up, to rest The violet's reclining head." (Donne)

definitions.text: A—bank swelled up, to rest The violet's reclining head." (Donne)

parts.words: A—bank swelled up, to rest The violet's reclining head." (Donne)
parts.note: a line from John Donne's poem The Ecstasy with one word blanked out, describing a bank swollen like a full belly

explanation.surface: A quotation from Donne about a swelling bank pillowing a violet, with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank: the missing adjective in Donne's line about the swollen bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Donne's bank is swollen like an expectant mother, so the blank is the word for being with child.

clue.text: Red spies may be spread abroad.

indicators.note: the letters of the words that follow may be turned into something else, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Communist agents might be scattered across foreign lands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' signals that RED SPIES can become another word with the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To scatter in all directions is to distribute widely, the sense of the phrase.

clue.text: It's in the paper — as part of the Births, Marriages and Deaths columns?

definitions.text: It's in the paper — as part of the Births, Marriages and Deaths columns?

parts.words: It's in the paper — as part of the Births, Marriages and Deaths columns?
parts.note: the deaths column lists the late, so its notices are reports of those recently dead, playing on the stop-press item in a newspaper

explanation.surface: A reader wonders whether an item belongs in the family announcements.
explanation.walkthrough: The stop-press item added just before printing; the joke is that the deaths column carries news of 'the late'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stop-press item is a last-minute report printed in a newspaper, and death notices concern people described as deceased.

clue.text: Hungrily eats up the birds.

definitions.meaning: devours greedily, an old verb sense

explanation.surface: Someone or something greedily devours the birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eats up' looks like the start of a sentence about devouring the birds, but it is its own definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb raven means to devour voraciously, and the large black corvids share the spelling.

clue.text: Given to show it's a stout one rou

indicators.note: turning a set of letters round reorders them, signalling a rearrangement of the words before

explanation.surface: A portly person is described as prone to showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text ends 'rou', plainly 'round', the signal to rearrange IT'S A STOUT ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone given to show likes to display wealth or skill pretentiously, the meaning of the adjective.

clue.text: Loathe to see sailor gaining award in tea-making!

parts.note: OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

indicators.note: making something of tea turns its letters into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone hates watching a seaman win a prize at brewing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' rearranges TEA into ATE; 'gaining' simply joins AB to OM.
explanation.definitionFit: To abominate is to detest or hate intensely, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Sword may be stuck into this blackleg poet!

definitions.text: Sword may be stuck into this

parts.note: a scab is a strikebreaker, called a blackleg in Britain

explanation.surface: Someone wants a strikebreaking poet run through with a sword.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites stabbing the blackleg poet, but the sword goes into its sheath.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath holds a sword when it is not drawn, so the blade is pushed into it.

clue.text: Loose tune fans go wild for?

indicators.note: letters that go wild are scattered and reassembled in a different order

explanation.surface: Music lovers go crazy over a melody being released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go wild' rearranges TUNE FANS; 'Loose' is a verb, to undo.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose a knot is to undo it, so the verb means to release or untie.

clue.text: A guilty pronunciation.

parts.note: pronouncing someone guilty, a judge's verdict, punning on pronunciation and pronouncement

explanation.surface: Someone speaks a word in a shamefaced way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pronunciation' suggests saying a word, but here it means pronouncing a verdict.
explanation.definitionFit: Declaring someone guilty and sentencing them is a judge's censure of the accused.

clue.text: It could be a town to the north and in the north-quickly now!

indicators.note: the answer could be a town once a letter is added, so that town loses a letter to give it

parts.note: Preston is a town in Lancashire, in the north of England

explanation.surface: A musician is told a northern town would be the place to play quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer with N (north) put at the end would be PRESTON, a Lancashire town in the north of England; 'now' just adds urgency.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical direction presto tells players to perform very fast.

clue.text: Though there's water all round, it undoubtedly proclaims, itself to be terra firma.

definitions.text: Though there's water all round, it undoubtedly proclaims, itself to be terra firma.

parts.words: Though there's water all round, it undoubtedly proclaims, itself to be terra firma.
parts.note: a piece of ground surrounded by sea whose name split in two says it is dry ground

explanation.surface: Something surrounded by sea insists it is solid ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as IS LAND: it declares itself to be land (terra firma, Latin for solid ground) though water surrounds it.
explanation.definitionFit: A body of land surrounded by water on every side, whose own spelling announces it is dry ground.

clue.text: Young blood from South America, enough to eat.

indicators.note: the word from places the young blood after its origin, so the country comes first

parts.note: Brazil is the largest country in South America
a nut is old slang for a dashing young man about town

explanation.surface: A young man from South America has plenty of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Young blood' is old slang for a fashionable young man, also called a nut; he comes 'from' Brazil, so BRAZIL leads.
explanation.definitionFit: The large seed of a South American tree is a substantial edible kernel.

clue.text: Publication for children?

definitions.meaning: an edition of a magazine or newspaper

explanation.surface: A magazine meant for young readers.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share the word: one edition of a periodical, and a person's offspring in legal language.

clue.text: Welshman in a raid, risking his neck.

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the clue words that follow, spanning two of them

explanation.surface: A Welsh fighter takes his life in his hands during an attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' marks the name inside 'raID RISking'; Idris is a Welsh name, borne by the legendary giant of Cadair Idris.
explanation.definitionFit: Idris is a traditional Welsh man's name, so its bearer is an example of a Welshman.

clue.text: Model employer?

parts.note: not an ideal boss but someone who hires people to sit for portraits

explanation.surface: Asking about an exemplary boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model employer' usually means an exemplary boss; here it is one who employs models, a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter or sculptor hires sitters to pose for their work.

clue.text: Lose a car in a stretch of water.

indicators.note: the letters of the words before are set out in the form of something else, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone loses their car to the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of LOSE A CAR are rearranged; the Coral Sea lies off north-east Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Coral Sea is a large part of the South Pacific, so it is an example of a body of water.

clue.text: Strange to see how a good — and feasting reconciles everybody." (Pepys)

definitions.text: Strange to see how a good — and feasting reconciles everybody." (Pepys)

parts.words: Strange to see how a good — and feasting reconciles everybody." (Pepys)
parts.note: a line from Samuel Pepys's diary with one word blanked out, about a meal making peace among guests

explanation.surface: A quotation from Pepys on how good food makes friends of everyone, with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank: the missing noun in Pepys's diary line about good eating bringing peace.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepys names the main meal of the day, which with feasting brings everyone together.

clue.text: Space-traveller assembling radio set.

indicators.note: assembling puts parts together in a new arrangement, so the letters are rebuilt

explanation.surface: An astronaut is putting together a wireless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assembling' rearranges RADIO SET.
explanation.definitionFit: A minor planet orbits the Sun, so it travels through space.
